rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccan surah has 111 verses; a report from Ubayy quoting the Prophet urges teaching Sūrat Yūsuf to children and says reciting and teaching it eases a Muslim's death agonies.
rows.anchor: وفي خبر أبي عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: علموا أبناءكم سورة يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding surah closed with prophetic narratives, so this one opens by identifying those narratives as signs of the manifest Book and announcing its revelation and Joseph's story.
rows.anchor: ولما ختم السورة بذكر القصص، وذكر في السورة قصص الأنبياء، افتتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read the rāʾ of alif-lām-rāʾ with kasra; Abū Jaʿfar, Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, ʿĀṣim, and Yaʿqūb with fatḥa; Ibn ʿĀmir between them.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو، وحمزة، والكسائي: (الر) بكسر الراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alif-lām-rāʾ is not counted as a verse because it has two letters and does not match verse endings; Ṭā-Hā is counted because it does.
rows.anchor: قلنا: لأنه على حرفين، ولا يشاكل رؤوس الآي، وعد (طه)؛ لأنه يشاكل رؤوس الآي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An āyah is a proof or sign; bayān is making a meaning distinct and clear, from separation or disclosure.
rows.anchor: الآية: الحجة والعلامة. والبيان: إظهار المعنى بما يفصله عن غيره

rows.speaker: أبو علي وأبو هاشم
rows.claim: They define bayān as proofs; al-Jishumī approves this and rejects Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Baṣrī's definition as acquired knowledge, since that is tabyīn.
rows.anchor: واختلفوا فقيل: البيان الأدلة، عن أبي علي، وأبي هاشم وهو صحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAql is knowledge, including necessary knowledge that makes a person accountable; its root means restraint, since reason restrains vice or supports inference as a tether restrains a camel.
rows.anchor: والعقل: العلم، والعقل: علوم ضرورية إذا حصلت صار مكلفا، وأصل العقل المنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alif-lām-rāʾ is nominative as a subject whose predicate is tilka āyāt, or it may predicate an omitted subject meaning 'this is alif-lām-rāʾ.'
rows.anchor: (الر) محله رفع؛ لأنه ابتداء وخبره تلك آيات وقيل: خبر ابتداء محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In bimā awḥaynā, mā is a verbal noun, meaning 'by Our revealing'; hādhā al-Qurʾān has three possible parses, the first accusative as the object of revelation.
rows.anchor: (ما) في قوله: (بما أوحينا إليك) (ما) المصدر أي: بإيحائنا

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وابن عامر
rows.claim: They read yā abati with fatḥa on the tāʾ throughout the Qurʾān; the other readers use kasra.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر وابن عامر: يا أبت بفتح التاء في جميع القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kasra reading deletes the possessive yāʾ and signals it with kasra; fatḥa deletes the alif from yā abatah; al-Farrāʾ alone permits nominative tāʾ.
rows.anchor: الأول: كسر التاء، وعليه أكثر القراء على حذف ياء الإضافة، ودلالة الكسرة على المحذوف.

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr pauses on hāʾ in yā abati as a substitute for possessive yāʾ; the others and Yaʿqūb retain tāʾ, also permitted because yāʾ is implicit.
rows.anchor: فوقف ابن كثير على الهاء، ويقول: بدلا من ياء الإضافة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar reads the ʿayn of aḥada ʿashara with sukūn; the other readers use fatḥa.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر: أحد عشر ساكنة العين، والباقون بفتحها

rows.speaker: حفص
rows.claim: Ḥafṣ reads yā bunayya with fatḥa on the yāʾ throughout the Qurʾān; the rest use kasra to indicate a deleted yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حفص: يابني بفتح الياء جميع القرآن

rows.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
rows.claim: The usual reading has ḍamma on the sīn of Yūsuf, while Ṭalḥa b. Muṣarrif uses kasra; the name is disputed as Hebrew or Arabic, and both vowels are dialectal, as with Yūnus.
rows.anchor: وعن طلحة بن مصرف بكسر السين، وقيل: إنه اسم عبري، وقيل: عربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kawkab and najm are synonymous; sujūd means submission, kayd is seeking a stratagem, and ijtibāʾ is selection, likened to collecting water in a basin.
rows.anchor: الكوكب والنجم من النظائر، وجمعه: كواكب، والسجود: الخضوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idh is accusative with an implied udhkur ('remember when'); al-Zajjāj instead connects it to 'We recount to you,' while another parse connects it to 'you were heedless.'
rows.anchor: قلنا: نصب بتقدير اذكر إذ قال، وقيل: نقص عليك إذ قال يوسف، عن الزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kawkaban is accusative as specification; the sun and moon take masculine plural sājdīn because describing them with human prostration makes their verb follow human forms.
rows.anchor: كوكبا نصب على التمييز، وقوله: والشمس والقمر رأيتهم لي ساجدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yā bunayya contains three yāʾs—the diminutive, root, and possessive yāʾ—with one deleted, another assimilated, and kasra signaling the deletion.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: يابني ثلاث ياءات: ياء التصغير، وياء الأصل، وياء الإضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yakīdū is subjunctive as the response to the prohibition lā taquṣṣu; laka is either an optional preposition or means 'for your sake,' and kaydan is an emphatic cognate accusative.
rows.anchor: و (يكيدوا) محله نصب؛ لأنه جواب النهي في قوله: لا تقصص.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in laka may be connective, as in the paired expressions 'I advised you' and 'I advised for you,' or may mean that they scheme for your sake.
rows.anchor: لك قيل: اللام صلة، أي: يكيدوك، كقوله: (لربهم يرهبون)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kaydan is an accusative verbal noun used for emphasis, like saying 'he struck him a striking.'
rows.anchor: وكيدا نصب على المصدر، وذكره تأكيدا، كقولهم: ضربه ضربا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kāf in ka-dhālika is a simile: as God showed Joseph the dream, so He chooses him; Ibrāhīm and Isḥāq are appositional to abawayk and are indeclinable names.
rows.anchor: والكاف في قوله: وكذلك يجتبيك ربك كاف التشبيه، أي كما أراك في المنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph is told to remember when he spoke to his father Jacob; a prophetic report calls him the noble son of a noble son of a noble son of a noble son.
rows.anchor: وروي عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - أنه قال: الكريم بن الكريم بن الكريم بن الكريم يوسف

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads āyah in the singular, focusing on Joseph's story; the rest read āyāt because the many aspects of the story are each signs.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير: لقد كان في يوسف وإخوته آية بغير ألف على واحدة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر ونافع
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and Nāfiʿ read ghiyābāt in the two occurrences; the others read singular ghiyābah in both.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر ونافع: غيابات الجب على الجمع في الحرفين

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: The common yal-taqiṭ-hu uses yāʾ to refer to 'some'; al-Ḥasan reads with tāʾ referring to the caravan.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن بالتاء كناية عن السيارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUṣbah is a mutually supporting group, variously defined as one to ten, fifteen, or forty, or a word without a singular like raht.
rows.anchor: العصبة: الجماعة التي يتعصب بعضها ببعض، ومنه: العصبة أقرباء الرجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghiyābah is a hidden place or anything that conceals; it derives from ghayb and can mean a depression in the land, with a poetic witness from al-Munkhal.
rows.anchor: والغيابة: الموضع الذي يغيب فيه صاحبه، وكل ما غيب شيئا عن الحس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A jubb is an unlined well dug down to water, from the root meaning cutting; the verse links its root to the verb for cutting rock in the valley, and al-Aʿshā gives a well-poem example.
rows.anchor: والجب: البئر الذي لم يطو؛ لأنه قطع عنها ترابها حتى بلغ الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iltiqāṭ is picking something up from a road, hence luqaṭah for found property and laqīṭ for an abandoned child.
rows.anchor: والالتقاط: تناول الشيء من الطريق، ومنه: اللقطة للمتاع، واللقيط للصبيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophethood is not something earned as a right.
rows.anchor: وتدل على أن النبوة ليست بمستحقة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More than one prophet may exist at one time.
rows.anchor: وتدل على جواز أنبياء في وقت واحد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At times one should conceal a virtue to avoid envy; the grandfather counts as a father, as Abū Ḥanīfa holds in inheritance with siblings.
rows.anchor: وتدل على أنه قد يجب في بعض الأوقات إخفاء فضيلة؛ تحرزا من الحسود.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan can influence schemes through whispering, contrary to Abū ʿAlī's view.
rows.anchor: وتدل على أن للشيطان تأثيرا في المكائد وهو وسوسته، خلاف ما يقوله أبو علي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses imply that repentance after proposing murder is valid, since God reports their conduct without condemning repentance itself.
rows.anchor: عنهم، ولم ينكر. وتدل على أنه لا يجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Parents should not display favoritism that triggers conflict and envy, though preference for a sound reason is permissible; al-Ḥasan says envy harms only when expressed by hand or tongue.
rows.anchor: وتدل على أنه لا يجوز للآباء إظهار الميل إلى بعض أولادهم حتى لا يؤدي ذلك إلى فتنة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar reads taʾmannā with a doubled nūn and no ishmām; the seven readers use ishmām to signal the original two nūns of taʾmannannā.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر: تأمنا مشددة النون من غير إشمام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source lists four forms: both nūns pronounced, assimilation without ishmām, assimilation with ishmām, and kasra on tāʾ; it selects assimilation with ishmām as the reading.
rows.anchor: وفيه أربعة أوجه: (تأمننا) بالإظهار على الأصل؛ لأن النون من كلمتين

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads nartaʿ and nalʿab with plural nūn, attributing both grazing and play to the brothers, and uses kasra in nartaʿ.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير بالنون فيهما نرتع ونلعب أضاف الفعل إليهم جميعا

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: They read both verbs with plural nūn and jussive ʿayn; when asked how prophets could play, Abū ʿAmr replied they were not prophets then.
rows.anchor: الثاني: قرأ ابن عامر وأبو عمرو بالنون فيهما، وجزم العين

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr explains that the brothers were not prophets at that time, answering an objection to their saying 'we will play.'
rows.anchor: قال: قيل: لأبي عمرو: وكيف يقرأ (نلعب)، وهم أنبياء؟ قال: لم يكونوا يومئذ أنبياء.

rows.speaker: حمزة وعاصم والكسائي
rows.claim: They read both verbs with yāʾ and jussive ʿayn, attributing the actions to Joseph.
rows.anchor: الثالث: قرأ حمزة وعاصم والكسائي بالياء فيهما، وجزم العين أضافهما إلى يوسف.

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر ونافع
rows.claim: They read both verbs with yāʾ, and read yartaʿ with kasra on the ʿayn, attributing the actions to Joseph.
rows.anchor: الرابع: قرأ أبو جعفر ونافع بالياء فيهما بكسر العين من (يرتع)

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: Yaʿqūb reads nartaʿ with plural nūn and jussive ʿayn, but yalʿab with yāʾ for Joseph; this is also reported from Hārūn from Abū ʿAmr and several early readers.
rows.anchor: الخامس: قرأ يعقوب: نرتع بالنون وجزم العين، أضاف الرعي إليهم جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jussive readings treat the verbs as responses to 'send him with us'; the kasra reading derives from raʿaytu with its jussive marker deleted, leaving the ʿayn's kasra.
rows.anchor: ومن جزم فلأنه جواب أرسله معنا، ومن كسر فهو تفعيل من رعيت

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر ونافع وعاصم والكسائي
rows.claim: These readers pronounce al-dhiʾb without hamza; the others pronounce it with hamza, and both are dialect forms.
rows.anchor: قرأ الذيب بترك الهمز أبو جعفر ونافع وعاصم والكسائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for wolf may derive from a wind coming from every direction, as though the wolf lurks from every side; the source gives several plural forms.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أصله من تذاءبت الريح: إذا أتت من كل جانب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shaʿartu means becoming aware; the poet is so called for acuity, and the related terms refer to pilgrimage sites and their markers.
rows.anchor: وشعرت بالشيء: فطنت له، ومنه: سمي الشاعر لفطانته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The response to lammā is omitted, with proposals that their plot was grave, their aim great, or that 'they did it' is understood (Abū Muslim); grammarians also disagree about an extra wāw or making awḥaynā the response.
rows.anchor: قلنا: محذوف، واختلفوا في تقديره: قيل: عظمت فتنتهم، وقيل: كبر ما قصدوا إليه

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: The common reading makes ʿuṣbah nominative as a predicate; a report from ʿAlī reads it accusative, with an implied 'we gather as a group.'
rows.anchor: وروي عن علي بالنصب (عصبة) على تقدير: ونحن نجتمع عصبة.

rows.speaker: أبو علي وأبو مسلم
rows.claim: Al-mustaʿān means God helps me, and through Him Jacob seeks help against their account of Joseph; another view makes it a plea for strength to endure grief.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المستعان على الصبر في ذلك، عن أبي علي، وأبي مسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's tears do not establish the truth of a claimant; the brothers' race was permissible because it was not condemned, and Jacob recognized their lie from his statement that their souls had enticed them.
rows.anchor: تدل الآية على أن البكاء لا يدل على صدق دعوى الباكي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse teaches patience during hardship and seeking God's help; a report says ʿĀʾishah answered the slanderers by comparing herself with Jacob and his sons, after which her vindication was revealed.
rows.anchor: وتدل على وجوب الصبر عند الشدائد، ونزول المحن، والاستعانة بالله

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: The caravan was a passing group near the well, possibly coming from Midian toward Egypt; accounts differ whether the well lay beside the road or far from settlement among shepherds.
rows.anchor: قيل: رفقة مارة نزلت بقرب البئر، قيل: كانوا مقبلين من مدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water carrier is identified as Mālik b. Dhuʿr from Midian; another account has two men, Mālik b. Dhuʿr and ʿAwn b. ʿĀmir.
rows.anchor: قيل: رجلا من أهل مدين، يقال له: مالك بن ذعر

rows.speaker: قتادة والسدي
rows.claim: After Joseph clung to the bucket rope and emerged as a remarkably handsome boy, the drawer called out 'good news, this is a boy'; alternatives say he first saw him in the well (Abū ʿAlī), called a companion named Bushrā (al-Suddī), or announced finding a slave (Qatādah).
rows.anchor: فتعلق يوسف بالحبل، فلما خرج إذ هو بغلام أحسن ما يكون، ف قال المدلي

rows.speaker: مجاهد والسدي
rows.claim: The drawer and companions hid Joseph from the other traders to avoid sharing the purchase because he was cheap, claiming he was merchandise entrusted for Egypt.
rows.anchor: قيل: أخفاه المدلي ومن معه عن باقي التجار لئلا يسألوا الشركة فيه، لرخص ثمنه، عن مجاهد، والسدي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Joseph's brothers concealed that he was their brother and represented him as their runaway slave; Joseph went along so they would not kill him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أسروه، يعني: إخوته أخفوا أنهم إخوة، وقالوا: هذا عبد لنا، وتابعهم يوسف على ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: The traders concealed Joseph's status and treated him as merchandise, knowing that revealing who he was would prevent a sale.
rows.anchor: وقيل: اعتقدوا فيه أنه بضاعة، وكتموا حاله، كأنهم علموا أنهم إن أظهروا ذلك

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Judah watched from a distance, alerted the brothers after Joseph was pulled from the well, and they told Mālik that Joseph was their runaway slave.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب: كان يهوذا ينظر من بعد، ولما أخرجوه من الجب أخبر الآخرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows what they do concerning Joseph and all else.
rows.anchor: والله عليم بما يعملون أي: بما يفعلون من أمر يوسف وغيره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وأبو علي
rows.claim: One account says Joseph's brothers sold him; other reports attribute the sale to the caravan, or to those who pulled him from the well.
rows.anchor: قيل: إخوة يوسف باعوه، عن ابن عباس، ومجاهد، وأبي علي

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatādah attributes the sale to the caravan; al-Aṣamm says that if the brothers were present, their aim was simply to remove Joseph from their father for a price.
rows.anchor: وقيل: السيارة هم الذين باعوه، عن قتادة

rows.speaker: الضحاك ومقاتل والسدي والأصم
rows.claim: Bakhs is explained as unlawful, since the price of a free person is forbidden; other views call it oppressive or merely low.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حرام؛ لأن ثمن الحر حرام، عن الضحاك، ومقاتل، والسدي، والأصم.

rows.speaker: عكرمة والشعبي وأبو مسلم
rows.claim: They interpret bakhs as a small price; Abū Muslim explains that the amount was counted instead of weighed, as small sums did not warrant weighing.
rows.anchor: وقيل: قليل، عن عكرمة، والشعبي، وأبي مسلم،

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس وقتادة والسدي
rows.claim: One report sets the price at twenty dirhams, divided two dirhams apiece; Mujāhid says twenty-two, while ʿIkrimah says forty.
rows.anchor: فقيل: كانت عشرين، عن ابن مسعود، وابن عباس، وقتادة، والسدي،

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: The claim that Joseph's brothers were the people disinterested in him is rejected as untenable; alternatives are that the water drawers avoided buying him due to signs of free status or that sellers sought profit rather than sexual use.
rows.anchor: قال الأصم: وهذا ليس بشيء، وقيل: المستقون زهدوا في شرائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Karīm describes generosity; mathwā is a dwelling or place of residence, and ghalib is one able to carry out his will without hindrance.
rows.anchor: والمثوى: موضع المقام، والثوى: الإقامة، وثوى وأثوى أقام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ashudd means the completion of strength; it has no singular in its form, or its analogical singular is shadd, like ḍar for aḍurr.
rows.anchor: والأشد: كمال القوة، وقيل: لا واحد لها من لفظها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Miṣr is indeclinable as a definite foreign proper name but declines when indefinite; the kāf in 'thus' compares Joseph's establishment with his rescue from destruction.
rows.anchor: (مصر) لا ينصرف؛ لأنه اسم أعجمي معرفة، وإذا نكرته صرفته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose clause 'to teach him' connects to the preceding plan: God arranged matters to establish Joseph and teach him.
rows.anchor: واللام في قوله: ولنعلمه على معنى الكلام المتقدم، تقديره: دبرنا ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Mālik b. Dhuʿr brought Joseph to Egypt, where the Aziz Qitfir, keeper of Egypt's treasuries, bought him; another spelling is Iṭfir, and the king was al-Rayyan b. al-Walid, who later believed in Joseph.
rows.anchor: فلما دخل مصر تلقاه العزيز واسمه: قطفير، عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Aziz bought Joseph for forty dinars, a pair of sandals, and two white garments; Wahb instead says the auction reached Joseph's weight in silver.
rows.anchor: فاشترى يوسف منه بأربعين دينارا وزوج نعل وثوبين أبيضين

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: The buyer may have been an Egyptian, with 'of Egypt' standing for 'an Egyptian'; his wife was Raʿil, known as Zuleikha.
rows.anchor: واسمها: راعيل، عن ابن إسحاق، وهي التي تسمى زليخا.

rows.speaker: قتادة وابن جريج
rows.claim: Akrami mathwāhu means honor Joseph's dwelling or station; the wording honors him more than simply saying 'I honor him,' since honoring his abode for his sake raises his status.
rows.anchor: وقوله: أكرمي مثواه أعظم منزلة من قولهم: أكرمته؛ لأن من أكرم غيره لأجله

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Perhaps Joseph would benefit the household by managing their affairs when grown and knowledgeable, or by being sold for a good price.
rows.anchor: عسى أن ينفعنا أي: يكفينا أمورنا إذا بلغ وعلم الأمور

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: A report names three especially perceptive people: the Aziz in honoring Joseph, Shuʿayb's daughter in assessing Moses as strong and trustworthy, and Abū Bakr in appointing ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أفرس الناس ثلاثة: العزيز حيث قال لامرأته: (أكرمي مثواه عسى أن ينفعنا)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Joseph identified his ancestry to the Aziz, who recognized him as descended from a blessed noble household and asked Joseph to pray for a child; his wife then bore twenty-four children in twelve pregnancies.
rows.anchor: قال: أنا يوسف بن يعقوب بن إسحاق بن إبراهيم، فقال: إنا لله وإنا إليه راجعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God established Joseph as He had rescued him from the well and his brothers, until he held royal authority; one account says Pharaoh made him minister at age thirty.
rows.anchor: كذلك مكنا ليوسف في الأرض أي: كما خلصناه من الجب وأيدي إخوته

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Taʾwīl al-aḥādīth is variously explained as knowledge of the unseen, outcomes of affairs (Abū Muslim), religious sciences, dream interpretation, or all of these.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عواقب الأمور، عن أبي مسلم، وقيل: علوم الشرع، وقيل: تأويل الرؤيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's prevailing over His affair means He is able to do whatever He wills; the pronoun refers either to God or to Joseph, whom God protects and manages, while most people do not know his outcome.
rows.anchor: والضمير في أمره يعود على اسم الله، وقيل: غالب على أمر يوسف

rows.speaker: الأصم وأبو مسلم
rows.claim: They say Joseph became a prophet upon reaching maturity; al-Aṣamm treats his ordeal in the well as a miracle and allows a pre-prophethood precursor miracle.
rows.anchor: وأبي مسلم، وذكر الأصم أن ما كان في الجب وفعل به كان معجزة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Joseph was not a commissioned prophet is false because it conflicts with the Qurʾān and consensus.
rows.anchor: وهذا باطل؛ لأنه خلاف القرآن والإجماع.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowledge is among God's greatest blessings; the verse does not establish prophethood as a reward for deeds, since it may accompany good conduct as a benefit rather than become its reward.
rows.anchor: وقد استدل بعضهم بقوله: (وكذلك نجزي المحسنين) أن النبوة جزاء للعمل

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر ونافع وابن عامر
rows.claim: They read hīta laka with kasra on hāʾ and fatḥa on tāʾ; Ibn Kathīr reads hīʾtu with fatḥa hāʾ and ḍamma tāʾ, like jiʾtu.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر ونافع وابن عامر: (هيت لك) بكسر الهاء وفتح التاء

rows.speaker: ابن عمار عن ابن عامر
rows.claim: This transmission has kasra hāʾ, ḍamma tāʾ, and hamza on yāʾ, from hayyaʾtu laka; the same is read by al-Sulamī, Qatādah, and Abū Wāʾil.
rows.anchor: وقرأها ابن عمار عن ابن عامر بكسر الهاء وضم التاء وهمز الياء

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي ويعقوب
rows.claim: They read hīt with both hāʾ and tāʾ open and no hamza on yāʾ; the source calls it the familiar language and says it means 'come here,' also attributing it to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وهي قراءة النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم -، واللغة المعروفة، ومعناه هلم

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says al-Mubarrid recited a poetic address to the Commander of the Faithful with hīt as evidence for the reading; Ṭarafah's line supports Ibn Kathīr's reading.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر لأمير المؤمنين قال أبو مسلم: أنشدناه المبرد.

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو والكسائي
rows.claim: They rejected hamza; other reported forms include ʿIkrimah's hīʾt and readings attributed to Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar and Yaḥyā b. Waththāb, which the author calls unsatisfactory.
rows.anchor: وقد أنكر أبو عمرو والكسائي الهمز، ويحكى عن عكرمة: (هئت لك)

rows.speaker: علي وابن عباس
rows.claim: They are reported to read hīt with kasra hāʾ and ḍamma tāʾ, without hamza, like jīt; if tāʾ is ḍamma, it can mean 'I prepared for you.'
rows.anchor: ويحكى عن علي وابن عباس: (هيت)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Murāwadah means pressing someone to do an act, from seeking pasture; in this verse it euphemizes a woman's sexual request and is not used for pursuing a debt.
rows.anchor: المراودة: المطالبة بأمر يعمل به، وأصله من راد يرود: إذا طلب المرعى

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim analyzes murāwadah as the reciprocal form of irādah, ultimately from the scout who seeks pasture and guides a group.
rows.anchor: قال أبو مسلم: المراودة مفاعلة من الإرادة وهو من راد يرود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intensive ghallaqat indicates repeated locking and strong securing; the root of bāb is traced to wāw through buwayb and abwāb.
rows.anchor: (وغلقت) بالتشديد من الإغلاق، وهو إغلاق الباب، ونقيضه: الفتح، وإنما شددت لتكثير الأغلاق، والمبالغة في الإيثاق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hīt means 'come'; it applies unchanged to singular, dual, and plural, masculine and feminine.
rows.anchor: وهيت: هلم، يقال للواحد والاثنين والجمع المذكر والمؤنث سواء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maʿādha Allāh is accusative as an implied verbal noun, 'I seek refuge'; aḥsana is a past-tense verb.
rows.anchor: معاذ الله نصب على تقدير أعوذ معاذا فهو مصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Aziz's wife asked Joseph for intercourse and closed the doors between them, door after door; reports count seven doors or distinguish house and room doors, and say she sought to prevent escape or discovery.
rows.anchor: يعني امرأة العزيز التي يوسف في بيتها طلبت منه أن يواقعها وغلقت الأبواب

rows.speaker: مجاهد وجماعة من المفسرين
rows.claim: They regard hīt as Arabic; it may mean 'come here' according to Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and Ibn Zayd, or simply 'approach' according to Abū Muslim from al-Mubarrid.
rows.anchor: عليها أحد، وقيل: هيت لك فيه قولان: الأول: أنها لغة عربية، عن مجاهد وجماعة من المفسرين

rows.speaker: عكرمة وغيره
rows.claim: They say hīt is not Arabic: al-Suddī calls it Coptic for 'come here,' al-Ḥasan Syriac for 'upon you,' and al-Aṣamm says it was her people's word; one explanation is that both languages share it.
rows.anchor: والثاني: أنه ليس بلغة عربية، عن عكرمة وغيره.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse requires refraining from every wrong to honor God's rights, permits restraint to honor others' rights, and calls committing sin injustice.
rows.anchor: تدل الآية على أن الواجب الامتناع من كل قبيح لرعاية حق الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person appearing in the role of a master may be called rabb; Joseph did not desire the woman or intend vice, since his words all show refusal.
rows.anchor: وتدل على أن يوسف ما أرادها، ولا هم بقبيح؛ لأن جميع ما في الآية من كلامه يدل على ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When invited to sin one must seek God's protection; this includes temptation by devils, human devils, and the self, and the acts of seduction and seeking refuge refute the Jabriyya.
rows.anchor: وتدل على أن الواجب عند الدعاء إلى معصية الاستعاذة بالله ليعصمه من ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وابن عامر وأبو عمرو ويعقوب
rows.claim: They read al-mukhliṣīn with kasra on lām, meaning people who devote worship to God; others use fatḥa, meaning those chosen and purified for prophethood.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وابن عامر وأبو عمرو ويعقوب: [المخلصين] بكسر اللام

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: The common qabl and dubr have doubled consonants; Ibn Isḥāq lightens them, and both are dialect variants.
rows.anchor: وقراءة العامة: قبل ودبر بالتثقيل، وخفف ابن إسحاق ذلك، وهما لغتان.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamm is an intention or approach toward something without entering it; the source adduces a poem saying the speaker intended but did not act.
rows.anchor: الهم: القصد، وهو مقاربة الشيء من غير دخول فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Burhān is a proof or argument, and istibāq is seeking precedence by racing toward something.
rows.anchor: والبرهان: الحجة، يقال: برهن أي: بين بحجة. والاستباق: افتعال من السبق

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن عباس
rows.claim: The usual muttakaʾ has doubled tāʾ and hamza; Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās are reported with mutka, light and unhamzated, while Abū Jaʿfar also omits hamza but doubles tāʾ. Abū Zayd says it is anything cut with a knife.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد: متكا خفيفة غير مهموزة، وروي نحوه عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr retains the alif in ḥāshā in connected reading; the source cites a poem beginning ḥāshā Abī Thawbān as evidence for the original form from muḥāshāh, meaning distancing.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو: حاشا بإثبات الألف على الوصل

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: The other readers omit the alif for ease and conformity with the codex; Abū ʿUbaydah says the ʿUthmānic master codex wrote ḥāsh without alif.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: قرأ بها في مصحف الإمام عثمان (حاش) بغير ألف.

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء العطاردي والشعبي والأعرج
rows.claim: The common reading has shaghafahā with ghayn; these readers use ʿayn, while al-Farrāʾ links the common form to love reaching the heart's covering.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي رجاء العطاردي والشعبي والأعرج بالعين غير معجمة

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: The common basharan is accusative either after an omitted preposition or as the predicate of mā; al-Aʿmash reads nominative, matching Najd and Tamīm speakers who do not govern mā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش: بشر بالرفع، وهي لغة أهل نجد، وبني تميم؛

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative reading is supported by two poetic examples where mā does not govern its predicate; the text quotes both lines as evidence.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر: شتان ما بيني وبين بني أبي ... جميعا فما هذان مستويان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿAzīz means one made invulnerable by power, and could describe the husband through his authority or be his personal name; fatā means a young man, while Arabs also call a male slave fatā (Abū Muslim).
rows.anchor: العزيز: المنيع بقدرته عن أن يضام في أمره، وكان زوجها ممتنعا بملكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ittibāʿ means following a track and seeking to catch up with the one ahead.
rows.anchor: والاتباع: اقتفاء الأثر، وهو طلب اللحق بالأول.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In tarzuqāni, nūn marks indicative mood; in subjunctive or jussive, the form would be tarzuqā.
rows.anchor: ترزقانه النون علامة الرفع، ولو كان نصبا أو جزما لقال: ترزقاه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq, and Yaʿqūb are indeclinable foreign names; repeated pronouns may emphasize or let the first clause serve as support and the second as the new sentence.
rows.anchor: ويعقوب) لا ينصرف شيء منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first an in the repeated construction can serve as support and the second begin the clause, with kāfirūn as its predicate; min in min shayʾ is extra, meaning 'anything.'
rows.anchor: وفيه (من) في قوله: من شيء صلة تقديره: ما كان لنا أن نشرك بالله شيئا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istiḫlāṣ means making something wholly one's own without a share for another; a report about Salmān uses khalāṣ for gold purified by fire.
rows.anchor: الاستخلاص: خلوص الشيء من شائب الاشتراك، كأنه يريد أن يكون خالصا له

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads ḥaythu nashāʾ with God's first-person plural, matching 'We established' and 'We grant'; the others read yashāʾ as referring to Joseph, matching 'he settles.'
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير: حيث نشاء بالنون مضافا إلى الله تعالى لقوله: مكنا ونصيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tamkīn is a station or standing through which one can manage affairs; tabawwuʾ is taking a residence to which one returns, from bāʾ meaning return.
rows.anchor: والتمكين من المكانة، وأصله من التمكين في الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article in 'the earth' refers to the known land, meaning the treasuries of your land.
rows.anchor: الألف واللام في قوله: الأرض للعهد، دون الجنس، كأنه قال: خزائن أرضك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After learning Joseph's trustworthiness, innocence, and knowledge, the king called him from prison and made him a close adviser in his affairs; makīn means empowered and amīn trustworthy, or firmly established in high rank and proven innocent.
rows.anchor: لما تبين للملك أمانة يوسف وبراءته وعلمه، أمر بإحضاره ليجعله من خلصائه

rows.speaker: قتادة وابن إسحاق وأبو علي
rows.claim: They explain ḥafīẓ ʿalīm as guarding the treasury from those not entitled and knowing how to administer it; other views say he knew its accounts and languages or could plan reserves through famine.
rows.anchor: قيل: حفيظ عمن لا يستحقها، عليم بوجوه التدبير فيها، عن قتادة، وابن إسحاق، وأبي علي

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says ʿalīm means knowing the ways the treasury can be managed.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عليم بوجوه متصرفاتها، عن الزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph asked for the position to benefit people through sound administration.
rows.anchor: وإنما سأل ذلك لصلاح العباد لحسن تدبيره لهم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Joseph's free choice of where to settle showed he no longer answered to the king.
rows.anchor: يوضح أنه كان لا يرجع إلى أمر الملك، وصار بحيث لا أمر عليه، عن أبي علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says Joseph's authority was reward for patience (Abū ʿAlī); the Qāḍī instead sees grace mixed with obligation, neither of which fits the definition of reward.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كل ذلك كان ثوابا منه على صبره؛ لذلك قال: ولا نضيع أجر المحسنين، عن أبي علي، وقيل: بل هو بين تفضل وبين تكليف

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم
rows.claim: They read li-fityānihi with alif and nūn, a reading also found in Ibn Masʿūd's codex and preferred by Abū ʿUbayd; the others read li-fityatihi, both being valid forms.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم: لفتيانه بالألف والنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jihāz is household goods or travel equipment; a fatā is a strong young man, with plural forms fityān and fityah.
rows.anchor: جهاز البيت: متاعه، وجهزت فلانا: هيأت جهاز سفره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Murāwadah is seeking or requesting, related to rāʾid and irādah; desire is a type of accident specific to living beings.
rows.anchor: وأصل المراودة: الطلب، ومنه: الرائد لا يكذب أهله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Biḍāʿah is a portion of someone's wealth, from cutting, as with the knife called mibḍaʿ; rahl can mean baggage container or dwelling.
rows.anchor: والبضاعة: القطعة من مال الرجل، واستبضعت الشيء: جعلته بضاعة، وأصل البضع: القطع

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says returning the goods made it easier for Jacob to send the brothers back.
rows.anchor: عليهم العود، وعلى أبيهم إرسالهم، عن الكلبي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph gathered information gradually and delayed requesting their brother to avoid suspicion; Abū ʿAlī says he wanted word to reach Jacob secretly that he was alive. Returning the goods was meant to prompt another visit.
rows.anchor: تدل الآيات على أن يوسف كان يسأل عن أحوالهم، ويتبع ذلك شيئا فشيئا

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read yaktal with yāʾ, meaning Benjamin measures grain for himself, like the brothers measure for themselves; the others read naktal with nūn for all of them.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي: يكتل بالياء، وهي قراءة الأعمش ويحيى بن وثاب

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم والأعمش ويحيى بن وثاب
rows.claim: They read khayru ḥāfiẓan with alif as a specification; the others read ḥifẓan as a verbal noun, 'best in guarding.'
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم والأعمش ويحيى بن وثاب: خير حافظا بالألف على التفسير والتمييز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rujūʿ is returning to one's point of departure and is also used of resurrection; kayl is measured food, and amn is a heart's assurance of safety.
rows.anchor: الرجوع: المصير إلى الموضع الذي منه خرج، ومنه: الرجوع إلى النشأة الثانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baghy is seeking; mīrah is food carried from place to place; ītāʾ means giving while ityān means coming; mūthiq is a binding covenant, commonly made by oath.
rows.anchor: والموثق: العقد المؤكد بالقسم، ومنه: الميثاق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥāfiẓan is accusative as specification or circumstantial, while ḥifẓan is a verbal noun; annexing 'best keeper' asserts the quality, unlike the specification, though al-Zajjāj allows both.
rows.anchor: حافظا نصب على التمييز، وقيل: على الحال، و(حفظا) على المصدر.

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Naktal derives from naktāl; its alif drops when two vowelless sounds meet at the lām.
rows.anchor: نكتل: أصله: نكتال، ذهبت الألف لالتقاء الساكنين اللذين أحدهما اللام، عن أبي مسلم.

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: In illā an yuḥāṭa bikum, an is accusative as a purpose complement, meaning 'except for your being surrounded,' as in comparable constructions about coming for money.
rows.anchor: قلنا: نصب بمعنى المفعول له، وتقديره: إلا الإحاطة بكم، كقولهم: لم تأتني إلا لأجل الدراهم

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو علي والأصم والزجاج وأبو مسلم
rows.claim: 'We were denied the measure' may mean they were denied extra grain beyond each camel-load, but the preferred reading is that future rations would be withheld unless they brought their brother.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن، وأبي علي، والأصم، والزجاج، وأبي مسلم، وهو الوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers say Benjamin should come so all can measure; the yāʾ reading specifically means Benjamin measures for himself, and they promise strenuous protection from harms.
rows.anchor: فأرسل معنا أخانا بنيامين إلى ملك مصر نكتل نحن وهو

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Jacob's challenge recalls that he trusted the brothers to protect Joseph; God's protection of Benjamin is better than theirs.
rows.anchor: فالله خير حافظا يعني حفظ الله بنيامين خير من حفظكم، عن أبي علي

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Aṣamm says Jacob meant God's protection of Joseph, whom Jacob knew to be alive.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه: فالله خير حافظا ليوسف، وكان يعلم أنه حي، عن الأصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings make Jacob's words an appeal for mercy or an expression of trust in God after his experience with the brothers.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ذكر ذلك على سبيل استنزال الرحمة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob sent Benjamin because circumstances had changed as the brothers grew toward goodness, because famine forced his hand, or because God revealed and guaranteed his safety; the revelation and guarantee is preferred.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه تعالى أوحى إليه بذلك، وضمن حفظه، وهذا هو الوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is most merciful to His creatures, pitying Jacob's weakness and age and returning Benjamin to him.
rows.anchor: وهو أرحم الراحمين بخلقه يرحم ضعفي وكبر سني، ويرده علي

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: 'What more do we seek?' means the Egyptian ruler measured fully and returned their payment; the brothers used this to reassure Jacob about sending Benjamin.
rows.anchor: قيل: أي شيء نطلب وراء هذا، أوفى لنا الكيل، ورد علينا الثمن، عن قتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suggestion that the brothers were merely delighted to find the payment because they were poor is called unsound; another interpretation is that they were not lying about the ruler's generous treatment.
rows.anchor: وقيل: استبشر بوجود بضاعتهم لضيق أيديهم، وهذا لا يصح

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the extra qīl of a camel may mean a donkey-load, since baʿīr can be used for a donkey.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حمل بعير يعني: حمل حمار، وهي لغة يقال للحمار بعير، عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'an easy measure' is variously glossed as little, easy for the measurer, easier when Benjamin accompanies them, or quick and not deficient; these claims support sending him.
rows.anchor: ذلك كيل يسير قيل: قليل، فنحتاج إلى أن نضيف إليه كيل بعير أخينا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Jacob requires a covenant in God's name, by oath or other assurance; one report says they swore by Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets, and later repeats that they swore by his standing with God.
rows.anchor: وقيل: تحلفوا لي بخاتم النبيين وسيد المرسلين محمد - صلى الله عليه وسلم -، عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Illā an yuḥāṭa bikum means unless all of them are destroyed; another explanation is that they are overcome and unable to fulfill the pledge.
rows.anchor: إلا أن تهلكوا جميعا، عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: القتبي
rows.claim: God as wakīl means witness and keeper of faithful fulfillment, or guarantor according to al-Qutaybī; a report says God pledged to return both sons after Jacob entrusted Him with the matter.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كفيل، عن [القتبي]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some claim Jacob still distrusted the brothers as persistent wrongdoers, but the author rejects this: they had matured, regretted their earlier conduct, and were no longer persisting.
rows.anchor: وهذا باطل لما ذكرنا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وقتادة والضحاك والسدي والأصم وأبو مسلم
rows.claim: Jacob feared the evil eye because his sons were handsome and impressive, all from one father; Abū ʿAlī rejects this explanation as unsupported by proof.
rows.anchor: قيل: خاف عليهم العين؛ لأنهم كانوا ذوي جمال وهيئة وكمال

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Another view says Jacob feared others' envy and that the king might hear of their strength, then imprison or kill them as a threat to his rule.
rows.anchor: وقيل: خاف عليهم حسد الناس لهم، وأن يبلغ الملك قوتهم وبطشهم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Jacob may simply have thought separating them safer against dangers; al-Nakhʿī says the separation was meant to let Benjamin reach Joseph.
rows.anchor: وقيل: خاف عليهم الغوائل إذا كانوا مجتمعين، فرأى التفرق أسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Precautions can help against people but cannot avert God's decree; one should not be deluded by precautions because caution cannot prevent destiny.
rows.anchor: يعني أن ما يريد الله بكم لا ينفع منه الاحتياط، وإن كان ينفع من الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception in 'nothing would avail them except a need in Jacob's soul' is an exception phrase; min before 'anything' is emphatic, meaning nothing could avail against God.
rows.anchor: (من) في قوله: من شيء، قيل: (من) توكيد، ومعناه: ما كان يغني عنهم من الله شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob instructed them to enter Egypt by separate gates; he knew caution could not counter God's will, and the direction fulfilled a personal concern in his heart.
rows.anchor: يابني لا تدخلوا من باب واحد إذا دخلتم مصر وادخلوا من أبواب متفرقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed evil-eye ray that affects its target like poison is rejected: it would not explain selective effects, bodies are alike, and bodies do not affect one another; even poison only kills through God's customary action.
rows.anchor: بمن رآه، فيؤثر فيه تأثير السم، وهذا لا يصح؛ لأنه لو كان كذلك لما اختص ببعض الأشياء دون بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The theory that the envier directly acts on another is rejected because bodies require contact to act, no contact occurs, and illness or death is not within human power.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو فعل العائن يفعله فيه، وهذا لا يصح؛ لأن الجسم لا يصح أن يفعل

rows.speaker: أبو هاشم والقاضي
rows.claim: The strongest account is that God customarily causes illness, alteration, or death on seeing and admiring something, for a beneficial purpose.
rows.anchor: وهذا أقوى ما قيل فيه، وهو قول أبي هاشم والقاضي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One should take precautions while entrusting every matter to God, rather than relying on precautions alone.
rows.anchor: وتدل على أن الواجب التوكل على الله في جميع الأمور، ولا يغتر بالاحتياط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āwā means going or bringing someone to a place; maʾwā is a dwelling or refuge, and īwāʾ means drawing someone close.
rows.anchor: أوى إلى منزله يأوي أويا: إذا صار إليه، آويته أنا، آويه إيواء: إذا صيرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The weak-looking letters in āwā can occur together because hamza counts as a consonant rather than a long or soft letter.
rows.anchor: قلنا: لأن الهمزة كالحرف الصحيح، إذ لم تكن حرف مد ولين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibtʾās means grief or distress, while al-siqāyah is a drinking vessel; Abū Muslim equates it with ṣuwāʿ, but al-Aṣamm distinguishes ṣāʿ from ṣuwāʿ.
rows.anchor: والسقاية: الإناء التي يسقى فيها، وأصله من السقي

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The common reading is ṣuwāʿ al-malik; Abū Hurayrah reads ṣāʿ al-malik, which many linguists treat as the same vessel, though al-Aṣamm distinguishes them. Other reported readings are ṣuwʿ and ṣawgh.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي هريرة: (صاع الملك) والصاع هو الصواع عند جماعة أهل اللغة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Faqd is an object's absence such that its location cannot be seen; tafaqqud means looking for an absent thing.
rows.anchor: والفقد: غيبة الشيء، عن الحسن، بحيث لا يرى أين هو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iqbal is turning toward someone face to face, opposite idbār; the source also quotes an unnamed poet using faqd of bereavement.
rows.anchor: مجيء الشيء على جهة المقابلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣuwāʿ is a food measure, with plural ṣiyān; ṣāʿ is also used, with plural aṣwāʿ.
rows.anchor: والصواع: مكيال الطعام، وجمعه: صيعان، ويقال: صاع وأصواع أيضا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥaml is a prepared load; the source distinguishes attached and detached loads by vowel and weight, and lists plurals aḥmāl and ḥumūl.
rows.anchor: والحمل: قدر من المتاع مهيأ لأن يحمل، والحمل - بالفتح -: ما اتصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zaʿīm, kafīl, and ḍamīn are synonyms for one who guarantees an obligation; zaʿīm can also mean a leader, as a poetic verse illustrates.
rows.anchor: والزعيم والكفيل والضمين نظائر، وهو القابل للشيء متضمنا بصحته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun for 'whoever brings it' may refer to masculine ṣāʿ or feminine siqāyah; ṣuwāʿ can be masculine or feminine according to al-Akhfash and al-Zajjāj.
rows.anchor: قيل: التذكير يرجع إلى الصاع، والتأنيث إلى السقاية، وقيل: الصواع يذكر ويؤنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tāʾ in tallāh is an oath particle restricted to God's name; bāʾ is the root form, wāw applies to outward nouns, and tāʾ is a branch of a branch, though another view derives it by changing wāw to tāʾ.
rows.anchor: والتاء في قوله: تالله حرف القسم، وحروف القسم ثلاثة: الباء وهو الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On hearing the call to stop, the brothers turned toward the caller and asked what was missing; the caller promised a camel-load of food to whoever brought the vessel and personally guaranteed the reward.
rows.anchor: ولمن جاء به أي: بالصاع حمل بعير من الطعام وأنا به زعيم كفيل، يقوله المؤذن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They were accused because they lodged alone in a house reserved for the king's messengers and the vessel was there; alternatively, its placement in their baggage or an informant explained the suspicion.
rows.anchor: قلنا: لأنهم نزلوا دارا منفردين لا يدخلها غير رسل الملك، وكان الصاع فيها.

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: The brothers said their reputation for careful, righteous conduct showed they were not corrupt or thieves; al-Kalbī adds that they had returned the payment found in their baggage, as thieves would not.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لأنهم ردوا البضاعة التي وجدوها، وهذا لا يليق بحال السراق، عن الكلبي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers had tied their animals' mouths on entering Egypt to keep them from crops and did not wrong people or trample fields.
rows.anchor: لما دخلوا مصر شدوا أفواه دوابهم كيلا تتناول حرث الناس

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: One account says the accusation was made without Joseph's order or knowledge; Abū Muslim says Joseph ordered it as an allusion that they had stolen him from his father.
rows.anchor: فجوابنا: قيل: نودوا لا عن أمر يوسف وعلمه، عن أبي علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Permissible stratagems can remove blame in a case like Joseph retaining his brother; the principle also supports tanning carrion hides, converting wine to vinegar, and contracts that render restricted matters lawful.
rows.anchor: تدل الآية على أن الحيلة في المباحات تحسن ليصير ما هو حرام حلالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse supports the validity of surety and guarantees, a reward for recovering lost property, and the rule that a guarantor bears the obligation.
rows.anchor: وتدل على صحة الكفالة والضمان. وتدل على أن من فقد شيئا يجوز أن يعطي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers are acquitted of this theft by their denial; their earlier act against Joseph occurred while they were young, since here they deny corruption and stealing.
rows.anchor: وتدل على براءة إخوة يوسف بقوله: (ما جئنا لنفسد في الأرض وما كنا سارقين).
